power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: CoBra: A Corpus of German Bracketing Paradox Phrases

text.text: This paper introduces CoBra, a Corpus of German Bracketing Paradox Phrases, and describes its construction.

It characterizes Co-Bra as a specialized linguistic resource that can be used both as a source of attested examples for theoretical work on adjective-compound modification and as an experimentally grounded dataset, in which each phrase is linked to the aggregated results of five psycholinguistic experiments on adjective attachment.
It explains how these envisioned uses informed the compilation process.
CoBra comprises 913 attested adjective-compound phrases drawn from sources published between 1822 and 2026, and is freely available for academic use.

Bracketing paradoxes are adjective-nominal compound constructions in which the morphosyntactic structure of the compound does not transparently correspond to the semantic scope of the modifying adjective.

They have long posed a challenge for theories of word formation and modification in German (Abramov, 1992; Bär, 2007; Beard, 1991; Behaghel, 1923; Bergmann, 1980; Burkhardt, 1999; Fabricius-Hansen, 1993; Haider, 2011; Härtl, 2015;  Institut für Deutsche Sprache (IDS) Mannheim, n.d.; Maienborn, 2020 Maienborn, , 2021;; Meinunger, 2014; Sternefeld, 2003; Wustmann, 1912).
text.formatted: They have long posed a challenge for theories of word formation and modification in German <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abramov, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bär, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Beard, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Behaghel, 1923;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bergmann, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Burkhardt, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Fabricius-Hansen, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Haider, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Härtl, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> Institut für Deutsche Sprache (IDS) Mannheim, n.d.; <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Maienborn, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Maienborn, , 2021;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Meinunger, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Sternefeld, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Wustmann, 1912)</ref>.

text.text: Despite sustained theoretical interest, empirical work on the phenomenon has relied primarily on small, often-repeated sets of canonical examples drawn from the theoretical literature itself, rather than on systematically sampled, attested language data.
This paper introduces the Corpus of German Bracketing Paradox Phrases (CoBra), a resource compiled to address this gap.
CoBra comprises 913 attested adjective-compound phrases, drawn from a wide range of genres and registers and spanning publication dates from 1822 to 2026.
The phrases are further linked to the aggregated judgments of five psycholinguistic experiments probing adjective attachment, semantic compatibility, and the effect of sentential context.
This combination of attested corpus data and controlled experimental measurement distinguishes CoBra from existing resources for the study of German compounding.
Nominal compounding is a highly productive feature of German word formation, and adjective-compound sequences are ubiquitous in written and spoken discourse.
The rightmost element of a compound is its head, determining grammatical gender and core meaning.
The elements to the left of the head are modifiers.
When a prenominal adjective combines with such a compound, standard grammar requires it to agree morphologically with the head noun (Burkhardt, 1999; Eisenberg et al., 2016; Fabricius-Hansen, 1993).
text.formatted: When a prenominal adjective combines with such a compound, standard grammar requires it to agree morphologically with the head noun <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Burkhardt, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Eisenberg et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Fabricius-Hansen, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: When the adjective's scope does not match this agreement pattern, the result is what is known as a bracketing paradox (Abramov, 1992; Bär, 2007; Behaghel, 1923; Bergmann, 1980; Burkhardt, 1999; Fabricius-Hansen, 1993; Haider, 2011; Härtl, 2015;  Institut für Deutsche Sprache (IDS) Mannheim, n.d.; Maienborn, 2020 Maienborn, , 2021;; Meinunger, 2014; Sternefeld, 2003; Wustmann, 1912).
text.formatted: When the adjective's scope does not match this agreement pattern, the result is what is known as a bracketing paradox <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abramov, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bär, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Behaghel, 1923;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bergmann, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Burkhardt, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Fabricius-Hansen, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Haider, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Härtl, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> Institut für Deutsche Sprache (IDS) Mannheim, n.d.; <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Maienborn, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Maienborn, , 2021;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Meinunger, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Sternefeld, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Wustmann, 1912)</ref>.

text.text: Here, the term is restricted to adjective-nominal-compound sequences, rather than to the morphological phenomenon in which structural boundaries conflict with phonological or semantic constraints (Härtl, 2013; Müller, 2003; Newell, 2021; Osborne & Gross, 2021; Spencer, 1988).
text.formatted: Here, the term is restricted to adjective-nominal-compound sequences, rather than to the morphological phenomenon in which structural boundaries conflict with phonological or semantic constraints <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Härtl, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Müller, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Newell, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Osborne & Gross, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Spencer, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: Consider illegales Aufenthaltsgesetz 'illegal residence act'.
Morphologically, illegales agrees with the compound via its head, Gesetz ('act', singular neuter) rather than the non-head Aufenthalt ('residence', singular masculine).
Semantically, however, the phrase supports two readings, given in (1) and (2).
In (1), the adjective scopes over the compound head, in line with its surface morphosyntax.
In (2) the adjective scopes over the non-head constituent.
The two readings share an identical surface structure and prosodic pattern.
The only difference is in the semantic bracketing.

(1) Canonical interpretation: illegales Aufenthaltsgesetz 'illegal act [regulating] residence' (2) Bracketing paradox interpretation illegales Aufenthaltsgesetz 'act [regulating] illegal residence' Despite this apparent irregularity, such constructions are pervasive across registers and interpreted effortlessly by native speakers, even though individual phrases vary considerably in perceived acceptability (Pryslopska & von der Malsburg, 2024).
text.formatted: (1) Canonical interpretation: illegales Aufenthaltsgesetz 'illegal act [regulating] residence' (2) Bracketing paradox interpretation illegales Aufenthaltsgesetz 'act [regulating] illegal residence' Despite this apparent irregularity, such constructions are pervasive across registers and interpreted effortlessly by native speakers, even though individual phrases vary considerably in perceived acceptability <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Pryslopska & von der Malsburg, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A bracketing paradox is not a surface feature that improved part-of-speech tagging or a larger language model could straightforwardly capture.

It is a mismatch between the morphological structure of a compound and the semantic scope of the adjective modifying it: identifying an instance requires a judgment about meaning, not merely about form.

For this reason, systematic corpus-based study of the phenomenon has so far been limited (Dima et al., 2017; Pryslopska & von der Malsburg, 2024). Dima et al. (2017) took a step toward closing this gap with a corpus-based model of semantic plausibility for German bracketing paradoxes.
text.formatted: For this reason, systematic corpus-based study of the phenomenon has so far been limited <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Dima et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Pryslopska & von der Malsburg, 2024)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Dima et al. (2017)</ref> took a step toward closing this gap with a corpus-based model of semantic plausibility for German bracketing paradoxes.

text.text: However, their work had several shortcomings: the model was built on a small set of items; the empirical validation was based on very few annotators; and the data was not released as a standalone resource.
CoBra extends this line of work into a large-scale, publicly available, annotated corpus with linked experimental judgments.

Three general-purpose German corpora could, in principle, be searched for Bracketing paradox candidates: • the Deutsches Referenzkorpus (Kupietz et al., 2023; Leibniz-Institut für Deutsche Sprache, 2025), a multi-billion-word corpus of written German covering a wide range of text types; • the Tübingen Treebank of Written German (TüBa-D/Z; Telljohann et al. ( 2015)), a syntactically annotated newspaper corpus; • the corpora produced by the Corpora from the Web initiative (Schäfer, 2015; Schäfer & Bildhauer, 2012), large web-crawled collections of German text.
text.formatted: Three general-purpose German corpora could, in principle, be searched for Bracketing paradox candidates: • the Deutsches Referenzkorpus <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kupietz et al., 2023</ref>; Leibniz-Institut für Deutsche Sprache, 2025), a multi-billion-word corpus of written German covering a wide range of text types; • the Tübingen Treebank of Written German (TüBa-D/Z; Telljohann et al. ( <ref type="formula">2015</ref>)), a syntactically annotated newspaper corpus; • the corpora produced by the Corpora from the Web initiative <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Schäfer, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Schäfer & Bildhauer, 2012)</ref>, large web-crawled collections of German text.

text.text: Each of these corpora is several orders of magnitude larger than Co-Bra and could, by virtue of size alone, be expected to contain bracketing paradoxes.

However, none carries the annotation needed to retrieve them: identifying a bracketing paradox requires a semantic judgment about which noun in a compound an adjective modifies, a property that no amount of syntactic or morphological tagging captures.
Nor does any existing resource link attested bracketing paradox phrases to experimental judgments about their interpretation.

Researchers wishing to study the phenomenon empirically have therefore relied on one of two strategies: manually curated example sets drawn from the theoretical literature, or ad hoc searches within general corpora.
Neither strategy supports systematic, replicable study at scale.
These limitations motivated the design criteria for CoBra.
The corpus contains attested phrases only, collected from real language use rather than constructed for the purpose of illustration.
It offers broad coverage of genre, register, and publication date, rather than reliance on a single text type.
It contains human and large language model-supported annotations for morphosyntactic agreement and semantic category, to support fine-grained analysis.
Lastly, it is linked to controlled experimental data, so that annotated properties and experimental results can be examined together.
The following sections describe how these criteria were implemented.

CoBra comprises 913 phrases, divided into three types that reflect different degrees of structural ambiguity and compositionality: bracketing paradoxes (3), ambiguous constructions (4), and canonical constructions (5).
This three-way distinction supports fine-grained analysis of the relationship between morphological structure and modification pattern within the corpus.

(3) Bracketing paradox phrase: fettiges Haarshampoo 'shampoo for oily hair' (4) Ambiguous phrase: geltende Rechtsnormen 'applicable legal standards' (5) Canonical phrase: rapides Waldsterben 'rapid forest die-off' Bracketing paradoxes form the largest subset.
Each phrase consists of an adjective and a compound noun written as a single orthographic word.

Where a phrase as cited in the source contained more than one noun or adjective, each combination was entered as a separate item, so as to preserve a clear mapping between individual constituents and compounds.

For example, palästinensische Ärzte-und Apothekervereinigung ('Palestinian Medical and Pharmaceutical Association') is recorded as two entries, one for each compound: palästinensische Ärztevereinigung ('Palestinian Medical Association') and palästinensische Apothekervereinigung ('Palestinian Pharmaceutical Association').

Similarly, roter, feinkörniger Sandstein ('red, fine-grained sandstone') is recorded as two entries, one for each adjective: roter Sandstein ('red sandstone') and feinkörniger Sandstein ('fine-grained sandstone').
While most compounds are spelled without an internal break, a small group of 15 unique compounds contains a hyphen (Table 1).
text.formatted: While most compounds are spelled without an internal break, a small group of 15 unique compounds contains a hyphen (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: For six of these compounds, the hyphen is likely unrelated to the bracketing paradox phenomenon itself: it marks a borrowed word (Hummus, Plateau, Sound), a proper name (Diana, Moulin-Rouge), or an abbreviation (DDR), all of which are conventionally hyphenated when compounded in German regardless of any structural ambiguity.
One further compound, S-Bahnfahrer, contains a hyphen because S-Bahn is itself a lexicalized, fixed form and its hyphenation has no bearing on the adjective's attachment site.
A further 6 items feature complex adjectival modification (Table 2).
text.formatted: A further 6 items feature complex adjectival modification (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: However, they owe their surface complexity to independent patterns rather than to the bracketing paradox phenomenon.
In frisch gepresster, gut erhaltene, and schnell wachsende, a manner or degree adverb specifies how the process denoted by the participle occurred (how recently, how well, how fast).
In blau unterfütterte, the first element is a color adjective specifying a resulting property of that process (the color of the lining), similarly to English resultative compounds such as blue-lined.
In rein äußeres, rein functions as a restrictive particle ('merely', 'purely') rather than a degree adverb, modifying the relational adjective äußer-('outer').
In all five cases, modification is internal to the adjectival phrase
The sixth item, CO2 neutrale Antriebstechnologie, is similar to the hyphenated nouns (e.g.
DDR-Linguistik).
CO2 is a fixed technical element forming a single complex adjective, CO2-neutral.
The phrases in CoBra were collected between 2021 and 2026 from a wide range of written, spoken, and digital sources (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The phrases in CoBra were collected between 2021 and 2026 from a wide range of written, spoken, and digital sources (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The original source materials span publication years from 1822 to 2026; where no publication date could be established, the corresponding date field was left empty.
The sampling strategy prioritized attested bracketing paradox phrases while maintaining diversity of genre and register.
Most sources originate from Germany (831), with a smaller number from Austria (6) and Switzerland (12), based on the author and publication source.
For 64 phrases the country of origin could not be determined.
The sources are split into 10 categories: lin-   , 2001) and Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (DWDS), 2023).
text.formatted: The sources are split into 10 categories: lin-   <ref type="bibr">, 2001)</ref> and Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (DWDS), 2023).

text.text: Further written sources come from published media (5.4%): newspapers and magazines, both national, regional, and specialized trade publications (e.g., Die Zeit, Gießener Allgemeine, Ärzteblatt, and Braut), books (3.5%), both originally written in German and translated editions, and peer-reviewed scientific articles from fields other than linguistics (1.2%).

Texts from public institutions (4.2%) comprise official, governmental, and academic sources, such as universities and research institutes (e.g., Universität Wien, Leibniz-Institut für Deutsche Sprache), governmental bodies (e.g., Land Baden-Württemberg, Bundesamt für Bevölkerungsschutz und Katastrophenhilfe), organizations (e.g., Bundesinstitut für Berufsbildung, Bundeszentrale für politische Bildung), and municipal or city publications (e.g., Berlin, Landratsamt Alb-Donau-Kreis).
Legal documents, such as court decisions and statutes, are included in the same category.

The corpus also includes commercial and everyday print material: product advertisements (8.1%), comprising descriptions of items, food packaging, and product categories, drawn from both online and print media; and posters and stickers (2.3%), originating primarily from Baden-Württemberg, including advertisements for events, billboards, school posters, and posters announcing changes to train schedules.
The second-largest source category is web-based text (17.3%), including forum posts, blogs, reviews, and personal or institutional websites.
Spoken materials (1.6%), including podcasts, talks, and songs, represent the only category not derived from written text.
Together, these categories form a heterogeneous, multi-genre dataset that reflects a broad range of registers and communicative contexts.
The corpus contains 969 unique nouns across 804 unique compounds.
Compound nouns were split manually into their head (N2) and non-head (N1) constituents and are recorded along with the compounds in the corpus.
The most frequently repeated nouns were Energie 'energy' ( 27), Sprache 'language' (21), Geschichte 'history' ( 16), and Buch 'book' (15).
text.formatted: The most frequently repeated nouns were Energie 'energy' ( <ref type="formula">27</ref>), Sprache 'language' (21), Geschichte 'history' ( <ref type="formula">16</ref>), and Buch 'book' (15).

text.text: There are 586 unique adjectives in the corpus, recorded as part of the phrase and in their base form.
The most frequent, deutsch 'German', occurs 31 times, followed by erneuerbar 'renewable', evangelisch 'evangelical', and groß 'big', each occurring 9 times.

In addition to the manual collection of phrases and the manual splitting of compounds into head and non-head constituents, each phrase was annotated for semantic category and for morphosyntactic agreement between the adjective and the compound.
Nearly all phrases (97.5%) are further linked to psycholinguistic data from five experiments on adjective attachment.

Adjectives and compound constituent nouns were semantically annotated using GermaNet (Hamp & Feldweg, 1997; Henrich & Hinrichs, 2010; Hundsnurscher & Splett, 1982), a lexical-semantic resource for German modeled on the design of WordNet (Miller, 1995).
text.formatted: Adjectives and compound constituent nouns were semantically annotated using GermaNet <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hamp & Feldweg, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Henrich & Hinrichs, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hundsnurscher & Splett, 1982)</ref>, a lexical-semantic resource for German modeled on the design of WordNet <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Miller, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: For each lemma, all matching GermaNet synsets were retrieved and their semantic classes collected.

Items not covered by GermaNet (105 adjectives and 28 nouns) were annotated with the assistance of Claude Sonnet 5 (Anthropic, 2026), a large language model prompted with a manually annotated set of 100 items as guidance.
text.formatted: Items not covered by GermaNet (105 adjectives and 28 nouns) were annotated with the assistance of Claude Sonnet 5 <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anthropic, 2026)</ref>, a large language model prompted with a manually annotated set of 100 items as guidance.

text.text: The model was instructed to assign each lemma a single category reflecting its most likely sense, rather than return multiple candidates.
All resulting annotations were manually validated by the author.
CoBra represents all GermaNet adjective and noun semantic classes, in either non-head (N1) or head (N2) position in the compound (Figure 2).
text.formatted: CoBra represents all GermaNet adjective and noun semantic classes, in either non-head (N1) or head (N2) position in the compound (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Many lemmas were polysemous (mean polysemy = 1.7): 51.1% of nouns (495/969, mean polysemy = 1.8 ) and 25.6% of adjectives (150/586, mean polysemy = 1.4) had between two and eight semantic classes.
Therefore, the category counts shown in Figure 2 exceed the number of unique nouns and adjectives, since a single lemma with multiple GermaNet senses contributes to more than one bar.
text.formatted: Therefore, the category counts shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> exceed the number of unique nouns and adjectives, since a single lemma with multiple GermaNet senses contributes to more than one bar.

text.text: The morphosyntactic agreement between the non-head compound noun constituent (N1) and the adjective in each phrase was annotated by two coders: a German native speaker and the author.
The agreement between the two annotators was 95.5%, with a Cohen's Kappa of 0.99.
Where the two annotators diverged, a third annotator, also a native speaker of German, resolved the disagreement.
Morphosyntactic match was annotated by comparing the adjective's surface inflection with the non-head noun of the compound, rather than with the head noun it is grammatically required to agree with.
In (1) illegales Aufenthaltsgesetz 'illegal residence act', the inflection on illegales is compatible with a singular neuter noun, matching the head noun Gesetz.
The non-head noun Aufenthalt is masculine, and therefore it is not a morphosyntactic match for the adjective, and the phrase was annotated accordingly.

By contrast, in internationaler Bestsellerautor 'international bestseller author', the adjective's masculine inflection matches not only the head noun Autor but also the non-head noun Bestseller, which is likewise masculine.
Such phrases were annotated as an adjective-N1 match.
A further source of matches arises when the head noun is feminine.

The feminine singular and plural adjective endings coincide in German (e.g., strong nominative -e), an adjective inflected to agree with a feminine head noun is also compatible with a plural reading of the non-head noun.
This is the case even where the non-head noun's compound-internal form, though recorded as singular in the corpus, is formally identical to its plural via the linking element.

For example, in landwirtschaftliche Maschinenfabrik 'agricultural machinery factory' and bevorstehende Unwetterlage 'upcoming severe weather conditions', the non-head noun's surface form within the compound coincides with its plural.
Such phrases were, therefore, also annotated as morphosyntactically matching.
The singular form of each compound was annotated rather than the form as attested.
Two considerations motivated this choice.
First, working with a single canonical form reduces variance introduced by number marking, which is orthogonal to the morphosyntactic match.
Second, it simplifies the annotation task itself, since annotators need not track separate judgments for singular and plural variants of the same compound.
Overall, in 385 of the 913 phrases (42.2%), the adjective is morphosyntactically compatible with the non-head constituent.
CoBra is linked to the aggregated results of five psycholinguistic experiments from Prysłopska and von der Malsburg (2026).
text.formatted: CoBra is linked to the aggregated results of five psycholinguistic experiments from <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Prysłopska and von der Malsburg (2026)</ref>.

text.text: Experiments 1-3 tested adjective-noun phrases in isolation.
Experiments 4 and 5 embedded a subset of phrases in a supportive carrier sentence (see Figure 3).
text.formatted: Experiments 4 and 5 embedded a subset of phrases in a supportive carrier sentence (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: The full methods, analyses, and discussion are reported in Prysłopska and von der Malsburg (2026).
text.formatted: The full methods, analyses, and discussion are reported in <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Prysłopska and von der Malsburg (2026)</ref>.

text.text: Here, I summarize the design and headline findings of each experiment as they pertain to the corpus data.

(a) Experiment 1: acceptability rating of the adjective with the non-head noun, head noun, and whole compound (b) Experiment 4: acceptability rating of the whole compound embedded in a carrier sentence (c) Experiment 2: forced-choice attachment: non-head, head, or unclear (d) Experiment 5: forced-choice attachment, sentence-embedded (e) Experiment 3: independent yes/no/unclear attachment judgment for each noun Experiment 1 collected acceptability ratings for each phrase in three conditions: the adjective with the whole compound, with the non-head noun alone, and with the head noun alone.

Ratings of the isolated adjective-noun pairs were reliable positive predictors of whole-compound acceptability, with the head noun carrying substantially more weight than the non-head noun; morphosyntactic agreement between the adjective and the non-head noun had no reliable effect.
Experiment 2 recorded which noun in the compound the adjective modified (non-head, head, or unsure).
Attachment preferences formed a graded rather than categorical distribution: 19% of items received predominantly non-head attachment, 35% mixed attachment, and 46% predominantly head attachment.
Attachment choices followed the semantic compatibility ratings from Experiment 1.
Non-head attachment was more likely the better the adjective fit the non-head noun and the worse it fit the head noun.
Morphosyntactic congruence contributed little to the interpretive preference.
Experiment 3 had participants judge attachment for each compound constituent independently rather than make a forced choice.
This allowed identifying concurrent attachment to both nouns.

Concurrent attachment was most likely when semantic compatibility with both nouns was high, indicating that some phrases support simultaneous rather than competing interpretations, consistent with the compound as a whole being modified.
Experiments 4 and 5 tested a subset (204 phrases) embedded in a carrier sentence.
Experiment 4 replicated the acceptability-rating task of Experiment 1.
Sentential context raised ratings overall but did not disproportionately benefit phrases with a Bracketing paradox interpretation.
Experiment 5 replicated the forced-choice attachment task of Experiment 2.
Sentential context did not shift attachment preferences, though it substantially increased the rate of 'unclear' responses relative to the bare-phrase task.
Taken together, the five experiments indicate that adjective attachment in these constructions is governed primarily by the semantic compatibility between the adjective and each constituent noun.

Morphosyntactic agreement between the adjective and the non-head noun played at most a marginal and inconsistent role, and sentential context affected perceived acceptability but not the preferred attachment site.
The corpus is available as a comma-separated file with UTF-8 file encoding at OSF.
Each phrase in the corpus is annotated with 36 columns containing linguistic properties, experimental results, sources, and additional metadata.
The columns are described in Appendix A. It is licensed for non-commercial, research-focused use, with attribution required in any publication that draws on the resource.
CoBra may be used freely for academic purposes.
As with any corpus, several compromises were required in the construction of CoBra, and these should be taken into account by prospective users.

First, the frequency distribution of adjectives and nouns in the corpus is uneven: the most frequent adjective, deutsch occurs more than three times as often as the next frequent one, while many items occur only once.
This imbalance reflects the frequency of Bracketing paradox-prone combinations in natural language use, but frequency-based analyses should be interpreted with this skew in mind.
The second limitation concerns the sources.
Examples drawn from the theoretical literature are over-represented, since this literature was the most efficient initial source of confirmed instances of the phenomenon.

This may bias the corpus towards examples that have historically attracted linguists' attention, rather than towards the full range of bracketing paradoxes attested in unselected language use, such as natural speech.

Moreover, some sources are no longer available, either because they were online and have since been deleted or because they were seasonal advertisements that were later removed For such phrases, the SOURCE and ACCESSED columns document where and when they were found.
Third, semantic annotation for items not covered by GermaNet was carried out with the assistance of large language models.
This subset is modest (17.9% of adjectives and 2.9% of nouns) and, unlike the GermaNet-covered majority, each item was assigned a single category.
While all such annotations were manually validated, users should treat this subset with appropriate caution, particularly for downstream applications that are sensitive to annotation error.

Lastly, a small number of phrases added to the corpus after the completion of the psycholinguistic experiments (23 phrases) have not been tested experimentally, and should not be treated as equivalent in evidential status to the experimentally validated majority of the corpus.
This paper introduced CoBra, a freely available corpus of 913 attested German adjective-compound phrases with Bracketing paradox potential.
It outlined the key decisions made during its compilation and annotation.
To date, no comparable resource exists.

CoBra fills a gap between theoretical discussions of bracketing paradoxes, which rely on small sets of recurring examples, and large general-purpose corpora, which do not allow these constructions to be systematically identified and compared.
The corpus' heterogeneity further supports analyses that reflect actual language use.
CoBra is well suited to projects on German nominal compounding and adjective attachment.
It covers attested phrases from a range of genres, registers, and historical periods, which supports analyses that go beyond idealized examples.
The corpus is annotated for morphosyntactic and semantic features, which supports fine-grained analysis of the relationship between compound structure and adjective modification patterns.
It also links nearly all phrases to judgments from five psycholinguistic experiments, so that annotated properties and experimental results can be examined in tandem.
The corpus can be extended in several directions.

Semantic annotation could be enriched with event-modification readings following Larson (1998), which would show how far the event structure of deverbal and agentive head nouns accounts for variation in attachment.
text.formatted: Semantic annotation could be enriched with event-modification readings following <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Larson (1998)</ref>, which would show how far the event structure of deverbal and agentive head nouns accounts for variation in attachment.

text.text: Adding Austrian and Swiss material would make regional variation testable, as at present the corpus relies on predominantly German sources.
Experiments with stimuli balanced by GermaNet category could test whether the semantic classes of the adjective and the two nouns predict attachment systematically.
Finally, although CoBra contains no frequency information, phrase frequencies and adjective-noun association measures from large corpora could be related to the attachment preferences.
In sum, CoBra provides documented, annotated, and experimentally tested data for the systematic study of bracketing paradoxes and related phenomena.
It can serve as a shared starting point for linguistic, psycholinguistic, and computational research on complex nominal modification, and for replication and extension of the work presented here.
Each phrase in the corpus is annotated with 36 columns containing linguistic properties, experimental results, sources, and additional metadata.
The columns are described in Table 3.
text.formatted: The columns are described in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>.

text.text: The lexical data is recorded in six columns.
The unique phrase identifier PHRASE_ID, the adjective and nominal compound phrase PHRASE, the compound itself COMPOUND as well as its' constituent nouns: non-head noun N1 and head noun N2.
Lastly, the base form of the adjective is recorded as well as ADJECTIVE.
The grammatical gender of the nouns is recorded in the columns N1_GENDER and N2_GENDER, respectively.

The results of the semantic annotation are recorded in three columns in the corpus: ADJ_CATEGORY holds the GermaNet semantic category of the adjective, while N1_CATEGORY and N2_CATEGORY hold the corresponding categories for the non-head and head noun of the compound, respectively.

The outcome of the morphosyntactic annotation is recorded in a single column, MORPH_MATCH, which holds a binary value indicating whether the adjective and the non-head constituent are morphosyntactically compatible.
The results of the five linked experiments are recorded in 17 columns.
The SENTENCE column holds the carrier sentence in which the phrase was embedded in Experiments 4 and 5.
AN1N2_PHRASE and AN1N2_SENTENCE hold the compound's acceptability rating from Experiment 1 (bare phrase) and Experiment 4 (sentence-embedded), respectively.
AN1 and AN2 hold the corresponding ratings for the adjective with the non-head and head noun in isolation, from Experiment 1.
Attachment results from Experiments 2, 3, and 5 are recorded separately for the non-head and head noun.
The columns N1_PHRASE, N2_PHRASE, and UNCLEAR_PHRASE hold the number of non-head and head noun attachments from Experiment 2's forced-choice task.
N1_SENTENCE, N2_SENTENCE, and UNCLEAR_SENTENCE hold the corresponding counts from Experiment 5's sentence-embedded replication of that task.
Experiment 3 asked participants to judge attachment to each noun independently rather than choose between them.
Therefore, its results are recorded as separate 'yes', 'no', and 'unclear' response counts for each noun.
For the non-head noun: N1_YES_PHRASE, N1_NO_PHRASE, and N1_UNCLEAR_PHRASE.
For the head noun: N2_YES_PHRASE, N2_NO_PHRASE, and N2_UNCLEAR_PHRASE.
The data source information is recorded in the remaining columns.
Two columns contain data about the phrase source: The SOURCE column contains a longer description of the source; the SOURCE_ID column a shorter source ID.
The date of creation (if known) and the date of last access to the source are contained in the columns DATE and ACCESSED, respectively.
Country of origin (Germany, Switzerland, Austria, or unclear) is recorded in the COUNTRY column.
Finally, the source category is recorded in SOURCE_TYPE.
